messages.subject: Re: Erratic results from secr.fit
messages.body_plain:
Following up on my earlier post:

The default value of the secr.fit details argument 'minprob' was changed to 1e-200 in secr 2.9.5, from 1e-50 in previous versions. I expected that this would affect estimates only in rare cases such as that reported by Valeria. We've found another instance in which estimates changed with the new minprob, and cannot be sure the problem with the old estimates is not more widespread. I still tend to think the problem reflects bad model fit, but there hasn't been a full diagnosis. If you're worried, refit models with 2.9.5 or later. For a complete check, try varying minprob in secr.fit(..., details = list(minprob = 1e-200)). Here's an example where 1e-50 was inadequate: minprob.pdf <http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/minprob.pdf> (note smaller minprob to the right).

Murray

On Sunday, May 24, 2015 at 1:29:20 PM UTC+12, Murray Efford wrote:
> I came across an issue when responding to a question on phidot that should be known more widely. Valeria Boron asked why estimates from a 74-day binary 'proximity' dataset changed when the data were collapsed to single-occasion binomial count data. Theoretically they should not change (Efford, Dawson & Borchers 2009).
>
> The problem was numerical (meaning, you can blame the programmer if you like). Essentially, model fits can be sensitive to the setting of the details argument 'minprob' in secr.fit. Set this to a small enough value and the estimates become stable. For example
> [code]secr.fit(CH, ..., details = list(minprob = 1e-200))[/code]
> seems OK, and in future versions I'll make that the default instead of 1e-50. It is possible that this may have affected other people's analyses. Always cross check your results! In this case I used some simple R code that calculated the likelihood quite independently of secr.fit(), and I'll look at ways to make that available.
>
> The data collapsed to a single occasion gave the correct answer and the original analysis was wrong.  I suspect it is a problem only with 'extreme' datasets (few animals, many occasions, and possibly poor model fit due to unmodelled camera site effects).
>
> (Incidentally: the likelihoods differ by a constant (the sum of binomial coefficients for each animal x site count) that depends on the data but not the parameter values; certainly the original and collapsed models should not be compared by AIC).
>
> Murray
